posts.author: ATT_Turan
posts.body:
I haven't done it, I don't work in the banking industry.
I think it would be a hard sell to convince a lending agent that your product is going to make sufficient sales to give them a good chance of getting their loaned money back.
Especially if any of them have any actual knowledge of video games and how few indie games make any substantial profit.

posts.author: bgillisp
posts.body:
From what I've seen unless you got a viable product ready to present to them, you are getting nothing for a loan. This gives  you a few options still.
#1. You can see if you can get a personal loan from a bank. Usually this just requires decent credit. But the interest rate might be an issue.
#2. You can use credit cards for what you need for the game. Watch out for those 18 - 59% interest rates!
#3. Kickstarter. This still requires you to prove you got a viable product and that you can actually complete it as the golden age of kickstarter is over. Too many got burned on flashy projects that didn't deliver what they promised in the past.
#4. Work an extra job and bank that $$$ towards your game. This will probably require giving up your game dev time for a while as you build funds. Hours could be an issue if you already got a lot of working hours, though you may still be able to take on contract work that pays you when you finish the contract instead.
#5. Learn how to do without spending any more $$$. This may mean learning how to code. You may need to learn how to do art.

PersistentDreamerGames said:

Click to expand...
That's really difficult to do.
Unless you were able to get in on the ground floor years ago and establish a name and following, there are very few people who can come close to making a living out of it.
Even some of the established indie studios that I've purchased stuff from - and sell a decent number of copies - talk about not giving themselves a salary for months at a time while commissioning assets for their next project.
Your best bet is to get really good at a skill (primarily art or coding) such that you can get commissions off of that skill, or get trained to not be working independently and be hired by a studio.

When I started people were saying it's impossible/crazy to sell an RM game and that only 1% of indie devs (as a whole, not just RM devs) were making more than 100k a year. So it's an urban legend that it was easier than it is now. Very few people were actually succeeding (as in, doing it full time with no other means of income). The reason is that most devs had to do everything by themselves (Steam was extremely picky back then and rarely accepting indie games).
There might have been some kind of momentary gold rush when Steam started to accept all games, circa 2014-16, and at that time anyone with a good game could have started and somewhat thrived due to much better (and far less random) exposure.
From my experience, that period was the actual best moment to get started. It didn't last long, though.

posts.author: Avery
posts.body:
If I was you and 100% commited (I am not, I would worst worst case go down the asset pack path for obvious reasons), I would probably search for game jams with a scope that fits my "real life" job.
That way:
- you build up a reputation and a portfolio that you can use later on, for example if you want to start a kickstarter or whatever you have "something to show" and experience under your belt.
- you learn to not only make but finish games and meet deadlines with the needed quality
- you can try out and learn things on a smaller scale of which you can benefit later on, if something does not work out it was just a small jam game
- if one of those really win something/get a lot of hype - you have the perfect base to build a commercial project on top of that
- also you learn if making one project after another and "having to do it" really is for you - there are many people who are great at something, but sometimes a hobby better stays a hobby cause making it your job could ruin it for you

I know a dev who makes a living off of games (not RM though) who reguarly enters jams to test out engines/systems/styles and get more visibility. Later there is often bonus content or alternate versions for patre-youknowwhat. It probably helps that he is a super good artist as well so his games usually leave an impression by default.
I would say as many other things "It depends", but generally I would not expect that making money off of games is fast enough profitable enough to make it a good option if getting food on the table is not secured.
On another note: I would especially not trying to get a loan for a game of which I have no idea if it can make me the money back. There are seriously so many free assets and plugins and whatnot out there (and packs for a fair price that you don't need a loan for), that I would if I wanted to try to move into that direction make my game as far as I can with what is out there and what I can make myself.
If you have a convincing demo and see proof that the game has enough people interested in, you can invest more into it or start a kickstarter that you use for those costum things.
Remember: you can swap out all art and music literally 5 minutes before release if everything is formatted right. It might make deving a bit more abstract or you might feel like it lacks something, but you save spending hundreds or thousands of $$$ on stuff for a game that might massively change during developing (and make some of them redundant) and makes you know you can finish the game before you put that much money into it.

posts.author: PersistentDreamerGames
posts.body:
The situation I'm in is, I'm getting older, large family , dead end job that is slowly disintegrating and isn't anywhere remotely aligned with game design. At best I get 30mins to an hour a day to work on game dev stuff.
If I try to build a portfolio of small games, even making a lundum dare length game takes 1-2 months at that rate.
If the goal is to build a backlog / portfolio of games, they need to be frequent enough to build an audience, if it builds an audience at all. Too much time between them and my games are lost in the shuffle.
If on the other hand I really buckle down on quality, then I've got a game that might be quality, but nobody knows who I am so it doesn't sell.
And sooner or later the fuse on the job is going to burn out.
I could just look for a different job, but then I'm investing time and energy on something that's 1) completely unaligned with game dev. 2) has a decent chance of not hearing back from anything 3) takes away from that small sliver of time I use for game dev.
Sounds like there's not really a clear way forward here.

posts.author: Dalph
posts.body:
OP:
Don't do this as your main job, you will
never
make a full living out of it, I hate to be blunt but let's be real here.
I think someone in this thread already mentioned it (forgot who) but my advice is to learn some individual skills first, like art or coding, doing commissions or selling resource packs\plugins is much faster and way more profitable than making full games.
Also IMHO it takes years to make a good and successful commercial RPG Maker game (to me successful means at least 10.000 copies sold), you can't make it in any less than 6 months if you care about quality and want it to standout. You also need a lot of marketing on social media and some degree of luck, it's not that easy.
None of the popular commercial RPG Maker games were made in anything less than 6 months. What will you feed your family with during development, uh? How will you pay your bills? There's also absolutely no guarantee that your game will sell enough.
You can make a commercial RPG Maker game as a side project, like what I'm doing right now, I have a main job and (very rarely) take art commissions for extra cash.
I don't expect to make a living with my game at all, but perhaps I can gain good profit\extra cash if I put enough effort with it and so can you.
Good luck! Think about your family first and secure a better job, then you'll focus on game development as a side and much smaller income. Then again if you get lucky and make the next Lisa, Omori, One Shot, To The Moon, etc. BIG kudos to you, but I personally would rather play safe, especially when a full family is involved.

It has not yet even opened.
Time can feel absolutely oppressive when you’re in a tough sequence of unsatisfying life factors. It’s common to look at an envisioning of the future and lose sight of the present. Sometimes people end up at the right place at the right time, but for most, a long term goal has to be comprised of many other much smaller goals and check points.
A lot of the time it can feel like “don’t do it, you’ll never do it,” but I think it’s much better to frame it as “there will be many experiences, failures, and triumphs along the way and you need a security net until you’ve seen it’s safe to cut it away.”
I think a lot of the advice in this thread is heavily pointing toward that, yes…most indie games do not pull full-time income. But. Y’know? Sometimes they do.
However,
the
common
outcome is that you’ll have to walk the walk of a new, unknown game developer and that’s what needs to be planned for and accounted for to secure your present wellbeing.
To circle it back to the original question of this thread, not even more money will guarantee the success of the game…at least not before more experience. I think that’s where the calls of making some smaller titles with more expectation management and getting them out there are coming.
Without getting those early experiences and early results under your belt first, a loan stands a greater risk of being a long term debt during a time where, from my perspective, what the present requires is more security.
TL;DR: It will probably be slower than you like.

Indinera's philosophy is similar to what I've seen from some self-published authors. They would regularly churn out books X times a month/year and were able to make a full time income after building up a catalog.
They also didn't like publishers because the publishers would restrict how often they could release books and tell them to change this or that.
Some of them went from being published by a publisher to self-publishing. They didn't sell as many copies without the publisher but made more profit because they didn't have to split it with the publisher.
Are you going to replace your job doing this? Not right away, but eventually it can after having enough titles.
